To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) informed consent is not required from all members of the community, (2) the community is the unit of consent, and (3) engagement is the key to success.

(1) individual consent should be solicited from those who are likely to be directly impacted by proposed gene drive open field research; and (2) community engagement should be conducted with those who are likely affected by such research.
informed consent is not always required for field research in the context of genetically modified mosquitoes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how informed consent and community consultation ought to be managed in the context of gene drive open field research.
the development of an ethical framework for gene drive research, with a particular focus on open field research.
the ethical conduct of open field research in general, and not with any particular gene drive construct.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

individual informed consent should be sought in all cases, but that this may not be practical or feasible, in some instances, and that in those instances where individual consent is not possible or practical, community and stakeholder consultation, engagement, and involvement will be essential to build trust towards the proposed research.

individual informed consent should be sought from all those who are directly impacted by the proposed field research, but that the precise manner of doing so will vary depending on local circumstances.
the solicitation of informed consent from individual members of host communities is not a requirement for the conduct of open field gene drive research in host settings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of a robust engagement strategy should be the first step towards any gene drive field trial.
informed consent and community and stakeholder engagements are both necessary, but not sufficient, for the conduct of ethically sound gene drive field trials.
gene drive research is not a special case, but rather a case that requires careful consideration of international norms and guidance on the conduct of human research.
The main takeaway from our work is that

informed consent and community and stakeholder engagements are inextricably linked, and that a failure to engage meaningfully with communities in the design of research protocols will likely result in the failure to obtain informed consent.

the solicitation of informed consent in the context of gene drive open field research is not a binary question of whether it is possible or feasible, but rather one of how best to engage host populations.
the solicitation of community consent and engagement are not alternatives to the solicitation and management of individual consent, but should be viewed as complementary to it.
